Doc Cheatham’s remarkable career in jazz reads like a fairy tale. Born Aldolphus Cheatham in 1905, he grew up in Nashville and took up the sax and trumpet at an early age. His first playing experience was at the Bijou Theater where he played behind Bessie Smith, later recording on the soprano sax with another blues great, Ma Rainey. His search for further playing opportunities took him to Chicago where he came under the spell of Louis Armstrong, eventually playing beside him and substituting when Satchmo was double booked. He devoted himself completely to the trumpet and became a sought- after lead player, performing with the big bands of Cab Calloway, Teddy Wilson, Benny Carter and Chick Webb. The demise of the big bands resulted in a new career for Doc, as he became a trumpet star with the Latin bands of Machito and Tito Puente. At the age of 60 he became the trumpet soloist with the Benny Goodman Sextet and later appeared with the Basie Alumni Band. He has been featured at Carnegie Hall with Wynton Marsalis and was the subject of a recent Nightline interview with fellow jazz veterans Milt Hinton and Lionel Hampton. Doc can be heard in New York every Sunday at Sweet Basil’s where he plays the history of jazz through his horn.
